analysis.one_liner: Restores the Glass-Steagall wall separating deposit banking from investment banking, insurance, and derivatives trading.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 8 cosponsors from three parties but never received a committee or floor vote; its last recorded action was a Senate Banking Committee hearing in May 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rebuild the Glass-Steagall wall that separated government-insured bank deposits from risky Wall Street activities until its repeal in 1999. Banks holding insured deposits could no longer affiliate with securities firms, insurance companies, or derivatives dealers, and the largest financial conglomerates would have up to five years to break apart. It also repeals special bankruptcy protections for derivatives contracts and adds penalties, including a fine of 10 percent of a firm's average net profits, for schemes designed to evade the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors and taxpayers, who would no longer have FDIC-insured deposits and implicit government bailout guarantees standing behind securities trading and derivatives dealing. Community and regional banks would also gain from reduced competition against conglomerates that carry an implicit federal safety net.

how_it_helps.text: Bars insured depository institutions from affiliating with, or being commonly owned with, any insurance company, securities entity, or swaps entity, so that government-insured deposits are no longer connected to trading and underwriting [S2][S3].

Repeals the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act provisions that created financial holding companies, forcing existing bank conglomerates to terminate prohibited affiliations within five years, with a limited extension regime that requires public notice from any firm that fails to comply [S2][S3].

Narrows the legal definition of the 'business of banking' to core services: taking deposits, extending credit, running payment systems, and limited customer-directed securities activity, while prohibiting banks from investing in structured or synthetic products [S3].

Adds an anti-evasion regime: any product or contract structured to dodge the prohibitions counts as a violation, and regulators can order divestment, fine the firm 10 percent of its average net profits over the prior three years, and open removal proceedings against individuals involved [S3].
Requires executives of bank holding companies to attest in writing, under penalty of perjury, that their firm is not engaged in prohibited activities [S3].

Repeals bankruptcy code provisions (sections 555, 559, 560, and 562) that give derivatives contracts priority treatment when a counterparty fails, removing an advantage that derivatives dealers otherwise hold over other creditors [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large universal bank holding companies, which would have to divest or spin off their securities, insurance, and derivatives businesses within five years, ending the funding advantage of combining insured deposits with trading. Some customers of those conglomerates could see changes in bundled services, and derivatives users could face somewhat higher hedging costs once dealers lose their bankruptcy priority.

drawbacks.text: Forcing the largest financial conglomerates to break apart within five years would be a major restructuring, and some banking services that customers currently get from one institution would have to be split across separate firms [S3].

The repeal of derivatives bankruptcy protections (sections 555, 559, 560, 562) would make swap and securities contracts subject to the normal bankruptcy automatic stay, which could raise hedging costs for ordinary companies that use derivatives to manage risk [S2][S3].

The bill allows regulators to grant limited extensions to the five-year breakup deadline, and requires only public notice from firms that fail to comply, so enforcement ultimately depends on the same regulators the bill aims to constrain [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but one-sided: the bill removes an implicit taxpayer subsidy to the largest banks' trading activity, at the cost of a one-time breakup that those banks could absorb over five years. The derivative bankruptcy repeal is the most aggressive provision and could raise hedging costs for ordinary businesses, but the bill's anti-evasion rules, executive attestations, and profit-based penalties give it more teeth than typical banking legislation. The biggest weakness is not design but the fact that it never came to a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee held a hearing a month later, and no markup or floor vote ever happened before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Introduced on April 6, 2017, by Senator Warren with original cosponsors Senator McCain, Senator Cantwell, and Senator King, and read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day [S1][S3][S5].
The bill attracted 8 cosponsors in total: 1 Republican, 5 Democrats, and 2 Independents [S4].
The only recorded committee activity was a hearing held on May 18, 2017, printed as S.Hrg. 115-57; the bill was never reported out of committee and never received a floor vote [S5].
The bill died in committee when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, without any vote in either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest universal bank holding companies came out ahead: they kept the 1999 repeal-era structure that combines government-insured deposits with securities trading and derivatives dealing, along with the market's perception of a government backstop for firms considered too big to fail. Taxpayers and depositors gained nothing, since the separation the bill promised never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large universal banks kept the status quo

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it as sponsor.

for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Sen. Mike Crapo

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee vote; after the referral, the only recorded committee action was a hearing, and the bill was never reported out.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan, with 1 Republican, 5 Democrats, and 2 Independents, but no votes were ever recorded, so the chamber's partisan divide on the bill was never measured [S4].

industries.note: The bill forces them to sever the tie between government-insured deposits and their securities, insurance, and derivatives operations within five years, ending the implicit 'too big to fail' guarantee that supports their risk-taking. Their interest in keeping that subsidy runs directly against taxpayers and depositors.

They lose access to FDIC-insured deposits as a cheap and stable funding source and can no longer sit inside the same holding company as a bank. Investors lose the cross-subsidy, but depositors stop backing underwriting and market-making.

Dealers are barred from bank affiliation, and the repeal of bankruptcy code sections 555, 559, 560, and 562 removes their priority treatment when a counterparty collapses, raising their cost of doing business at some cost to hedgers.
Insurers are barred from affiliating or being under common ownership with insured depository institutions, unwinding the bancassurance structures permitted since 1999.
They compete against conglomerates that enjoy an implicit federal backstop; separating insured deposits from trading narrows that disadvantage.
